html:
Performers
Royal Albert Hall Orchestra (orchestra), Edward Elgar (conductor) Documented

The label explicitly says conducted by Sir Edward Elgar; the composer credit alone was not used to infer this role.

[2] [1] [5]
Work version
Orchestral version Documented

The Elgar Society identifies this as Elgar’s first complete recording of the march, distinguishing it from the severely cut 1914 acoustic version. Complete does not establish that every written repeat was taken. The precise performing edition and organ participation are not established.

[2] [4]
Recorded
27 April 1926 Documented

Independently documented in the Elgar Society recording account and Naxos 8.111022 discography. Internet Archive’s date 1927 concerns the Victor issue, not the recording session. The identifier retains that issue year.

[4] [5]
Place
Queen’s Hall, London Documented

Venue is printed on the disc label; it is not inferred from the orchestra’s Royal Albert Hall name.

[2] [4] [5]
Label
Victrola (Victor Talking Machine Company) Documented

The label says Orthophonic Recording, identifying the electrical process.

[2]
Catalogue
9016-A Documented

Victor 9016 couples Marches Nos. 1 and 2; the January 1927 trade listing identifies the same performers.

[2] [3]
Matrix, take, sides
CR 336; Victor side 9016-A Documented

The specialist Naxos discography lists matrix CR 336-2 and original British issue HMV D 1102. The transferred pressing’s take suffix is not independently legible. Internet Archive’s matrix 9016A is the issue-side number, and its other ID CR331 is not silently adopted as the master number.

[5] [2] [1]
Transfer
George Blood, L.P.; Phoebe Pugh, transfer Documented

The item identifies the digitisation facility and user_transferred field; these are transfer credits, not original session personnel.

[1]
Transfer date
Unknown Unknown

The November 2023 upload does not establish the transfer date.

[1]
Processing
Digitised at 78 rpm; preferred 3.8 mil truncated-conical stylus transfer; equalised with turnover 250 and rolloff 0; MP3 derivative Documented

The original FLAC’s embedded comment identifies the selected stylus and equalisation. The site uses the supplied preferred MP3 without joining or changing the audio.

[1]
Composition rights
Elgar’s original 1901 march is public domain in ordinary life-plus-70 jurisdictions Inferred, not documented

Elgar died in 1934. This concerns the underlying composition, not an unidentified modern edition.

[5] [6] [8]
Recording rights
Territorial EU public-domain basis: Victor 9016 announced for publication on 28 January 1927 Documented

Rule 3. The Talking Machine World, 15 January 1927, p. 131, lists 9016 under the Victor list for 28 January, naming both marches and Elgar with the Royal Albert Hall Orchestra. This is publication evidence, not a session-date substitution; the British first issue may be earlier. Its 50-year term expired before the 2013 extension. US status is not established. The selected Great 78 item, original FLAC and label were checked; no NC licence or separate upstream digital recording is stated. The Naxos booklet is used only as documentary evidence: its commercial restoration is not the selected audio.

[3] [2] [1] [8]

Elgar, Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1 — Royal Albert Hall Orchestra, Edward Elgar; Queen’s Hall, 27 April 1926. Victrola 9016-A, issued 1927; master CR 336. George Blood, L.P./Internet Archive Great 78 Project transfer. Territorial EU public-domain basis; US status not established. Rights statement

OCR lines 24294–⁠24410 place the listing beneath that release heading; digitised bound volume talkingmachinewo23bill.. Accessed 2026-10-17.
  4. Elgar Society — Pomp and Circumstance, Elgar’s own recordings — 1926 first electrical and first complete recording, Queen’s Hall, Royal Albert Hall Orchestra; distinguished from 1914 and 1932 recordings.. Accessed 2026-10-17.
  5. Naxos 8.111022 — Elgar conducts Elgar booklet — Printed p. 5: March No. 1, 27 April 1926, Queen’s Hall, CR 336-2, first issued HMV D 1102; notes pp. 2–⁠3 discuss Elgar’s electrical recordings. Documentary use only; audio is not sourced from Naxos.. Accessed 2026-10-17.
  6. Elgar Society — Pomp and Circumstance introduction — 1901 composition, D-major march and G-major trio, later adaptation as Land of Hope and Glory.. Accessed 2026-10-17.
